title: Why No Garbage Collector?
story: Most languages use a garbage collector (slow, pauses) or manual memory (dangerous, crashes). XIOM proves safety at compile time — fast AND safe.
why: XIOM's ownership system achieves memory safety without a garbage collector, giving you predictable performance with no GC pauses and no manual free().
narrative:
## Memory Safety Without Runtime Cost

### Three Approaches to Memory

| Approach | Speed | Safety | Example |
|----------|-------|--------|--------|
| Manual (malloc/free) | Fast | Unsafe | C |
| Garbage Collector | Slower | Safe | Java, Go, C# |
| Ownership | Fast | Safe | XIOM |

### What Ownership Eliminates

```xiom
fn main() -> Int {
  // No use-after-free — compiler tracks ownership
  let v = Vec[Int].new();
  let v2 = v;          // v is now dead — can't use it
  // No double-free — only one owner frees
  // No null pointer dereference — references are always valid
  // No data races — borrow rules prevent concurrent mutation
  return v2.len() as Int;
}
```

### Zero Runtime Overhead

The borrow checker runs at COMPILE TIME. By the time your program runs:
- No reference counting
- No garbage collection pauses
- No runtime borrow checks
- No lock acquisition for thread safety

### The Trade-off

You must think about ownership while coding. But the reward is:
- Predictable performance (no GC pauses)
- Memory safety (no segfaults)
- Thread safety (no data races)

All guaranteed before your program ever runs.
analogy: Garbage collector = a janitor who cleans up after everyone at unpredictable times. Ownership = everyone cleans up after themselves immediately when they leave. No surprises.
try_it: Imagine this code in C: create a Vec, free it, then try to use it (use-after-free). In XIOM, the compiler would catch this before it runs.
tips: XIOM achieves 'fast AND safe' through compile-time ownership checks
No GC means no unpredictable pauses — critical for games and real-time systems
The trade-off for no GC is learning ownership rules — but the compiler helps you
Ownership is a zero-cost abstraction — it compiles away to nothing
common_mistakes: Assuming XIOM has a garbage collector — it doesn't, memory is freed deterministically
Writing code as if memory is unlimited — ownership forces you to think about data lifetimes
Overusing clone() to simulate garbage collection — learn to use borrows instead
